semin-durr:2-2.t:
His saying: {سجى}: It was said: its meaning is "grew still." From it: «سجا البحر يَسْجُو سَجْواً», i.e. its waves became still; and «طَرْفٌ ساجٍ», i.e. a languid eye. From it, «تَسْجِيَةُ الميتِ», i.e. covering him with a cloth, is borrowed figuratively. Al-Rāghib said this. Al-Aʿshā said:

4589 - وما ذَنْبُنا إنْ جاش بَحْرُ ابنِ عَمِّكُمْ ... وبَحْرُكَ ساجٍ لا يُوارِي الدَّعامِصا
(What is our fault if your cousin's sea surges, while your sea is still, not hiding even the small fish?)

It was said: «سجا» means "went away"; and the opposite was also said. Al-Farrāʾ said: "grew dark." Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: "its darkness became intense." The poet said:

4590 - يا حَبَّذا القَمْراءُ والليلُ السَّاجْ ... وطُرُقٌ مِثْلُ مُلاءِ النِّسَّاجْ
(How lovely is the moonlit night, the still night, and paths like the weaver's sheet!)

It is of the class of words with wāw as the third radical; it is pronounced with imāla (leaning of the vowel) only to agree with the verse-endings, like «الضُّحى», which is also of the class with wāw.

semin-durr:3-3.t:
His saying: {مَا وَدَّعَكَ}: This is the apodosis (jawāb) [of the oath]. The majority read it with doubling of the dāl, from التَوْديع (bidding farewell). ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, his son Hishām, Abū Ḥaywa and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it without doubling, from their saying: وَدَعَه, i.e. he left him. What is well known in the language is that وَدَعَ and وَذَرَ, their active participle, their passive participle and their verbal noun are dispensed with in favour of «تَرَكَ» and its derived forms; yet وَدَعَ and وَذَرَ have occurred. The poet said:
4591 - سَلْ أميري ما الذي غَيَّرَهْ ... عن وِصالي اليومَ حتى وَدَعَهْ
(Ask my lord what changed him from his union with me today, so that he abandoned it.)
And the poet said:
4592 - وثُمَّ وَدَعْنا آلَ عمروٍ وعامرٍ ... فرائِسَ أَطْرافِ المُثَقَّفةِ السُّمْرِ
(And there we left the families of ʿAmr and ʿĀmir as prey to the tips of the straightened brown spears.)
It was said: التوديع is an intensification of الوَدْع, because whoever bids you farewell on parting has gone to the extreme in leaving you.
His saying: {وَمَا قلى}, i.e. He did not hate you. قلاه يَقْليه, with kasra on the middle radical in the imperfect; and [the tribe of] Ṭayyiʾ say: قلاه يقلاه with fatḥa. The poet said:
4593 - أيا مَنْ لَسْتُ أَنْساه ... ولا واللَّهِ أَقْلاه
لكَ اللَّهُ على ذاكَ ... لكَ اللَّهُ [لكَ اللَّهُ]
(O you whom I do not forget, and — no, by Allah — whom I do not hate: Allah is your witness to that, Allah is your witness, [Allah is your witness].)
The object of «قَلَى» was omitted out of regard for the verse-endings (fawāṣil), since it is known; likewise after «فآوى» and what follows it.

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying: {وَلَلآخِرَةُ}: What is apparent regarding this lām is that it is [the lām of] the apodosis (jawāb) of the oath, and likewise in «ولَسَوْفَ». He the Exalted swore upon four things: two negated, namely His bidding him farewell and His hating him; and two affirmed and emphasised, namely the Hereafter being better for him than this world, and that He will give him what will make him content. Al-Zamakhsharī said: «If you say: what is this lām that enters upon "سَوْف"? I say: it is the lām of commencement (lām al-ibtidāʾ) that emphasises the content of the clause, and the mubtadaʾ (subject) is omitted, its implied form being: "ولأنت سَوْفَ يُعْطيك" (and you — He will give you), as we mentioned at {لاَ أُقْسِمُ} [al-Qiyāma: 1] that the meaning is: "لأَنا أُقْسِمُ" (I indeed swear). That is because it must be either the lām of the oath or [the lām] of commencement. The lām of the oath does not enter the imperfect except together with the nūn of emphasis; so it remains that it is the lām of commencement, and the lām of commencement enters only upon a clause made of a mubtadaʾ and a khabar (predicate); so a [mubtadaʾ] and its khabar must be supplied, and its origin is: ولأنت سوف يعطيك.» The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] transmitted from him that he said: «And its indication of the present was stripped from the lām.» End of quotation. Of these [two alternatives] that al-Zamakhsharī turned over, the one to be chosen is that it is the lām of the oath.
His saying: «It does not enter the imperfect except with the nūn of emphasis» — the grammarians excepted two cases from this. The first: that no particle of futurity (ḥarf tanfīs) be placed between it and the verb, as in this verse, as in your saying: واللَّهِ لَسَأُعْطيك (by Allah, I will surely give you). The second: that no governed word of the verb be placed between them, as in His saying, the Exalted: {لإِلَى الله تُحْشَرُونَ} [Āl ʿImrān: 158]. [Translator's note: in both cases the text reads «أن لا يُفْصَل» ("that … not be placed between"), yet both the verse and the examples show the lām separated from the verb (by سوف/السين and by إلى الله respectively); the intended sense is evidently "that … be placed between".] What I have said is supported by what al-Fārisī said: «This lām is not the one in your saying: "إنَّ زيداً لَقائمٌ"; rather, it is the one in your saying: "لأَقومَنَّ" (I will surely stand), and "سوفَ" has substituted for one of the two nūns of emphasis, so it is as if He said: ولَيُعْطِيَنَّك (and He will surely give you).»
And his saying: «its indication of the present was stripped from it» means that the lām of commencement, when it enters the imperfect, restricts it to the present; here that is not possible because of the particle of futurity, so the present sense was stripped from it.
The Shaykh said: «The lām in "ولَلآخرةُ" is a lām of commencement that emphasised the content of the clause.» Then he related some of what I have mentioned from al-Zamakhsharī and Abū ʿAlī [al-Fārisī], then said: «In my view it is possible that the lām in "وللآخرةُ خيرٌ" and in "ولَسَوْفَ يُعْطيك" is the lām by which the oath is answered, He having conjoined it onto the apodosis of the oath, namely His saying: {مَا وَدَّعَكَ}; so He would have sworn upon these three.» End of quotation. Its apparent sense is that the lām in «ولَلآخرةُ» is a lām of commencement not answering the oath, as shown by his saying secondly: «In my view it is possible». But the disconnection of this clause from the apodosis of the oath is not apparent at all, and likewise in {ولَسَوْفَ}; and al-Zamakhsharī's supplying a mubtadaʾ after it does not contradict its being an apodosis of the oath; he only prevented its being an apodosis [lām] entering upon the imperfect in wording and in implied form.

semin-durr:6-6.t:
His saying: {فآوى}: The majority read «آوى» with an alif after the hamza, as a quadriliteral, from آواه يُؤْوِيْهِ (he gave him shelter). Abū al-Ashhab [read] «فأوى» as a triliteral. Al-Zamakhsharī said: «It has two meanings: either from "أواه" in the sense of "آواه" — one of the herdsmen was heard saying: "أين آوي هذه" (where shall I shelter these?) — or from أوى له, when he took pity on him.» End of quotation. On the second [meaning] is his saying:
4594 - أراني - ولا كفرانَ لله - أيَّةُ ... لنفسي لقد طالَبْتُ غيرَ مُنيلِ
(I see myself — and no ingratitude to Allah — out of pity for myself: I have indeed made demands of one who does not give.)
i.e. out of pity for myself. The point of evidence in his saying: «saying: أين آوي هذه» is that had it been from the quadriliteral he would have said «أُؤْوي» with ḍamma on the first hamza and sukūn on the second, because it is the imperfect of «آوى» like أَكْرَمَ; this ḍamma-voweled hamza is the imperfect prefix, and the second is the first radical of the word, while the hamza of أَفْعَل is omitted according to the rule. This hamza was not replaced, as it was replaced in «أُوْمِنُ أنا», lest it become heavy through assimilation; that is why the Qurʾān readers stipulated that «تُؤْويه» in His saying «وفَصيلتِه التي تُؤْويه» may not be replaced, because of the heaviness.

semin-durr:8-8.t:
His saying: {عَآئِلاً}, i.e. poor. This is the reading of the majority. One says: عال زيدٌ, i.e. he became poor. Jarīr said:
4595 - اللهُ نَزَّل في الكتابِ فريضةً ... لابنِ السبيل وللفقيرِ العائلِ
(Allah sent down in the Book an obligatory share for the wayfarer and for the needy poor.)
And أعال: his dependants became many. He said:
4596 - ومايَدْري الفقيرُ متى غِناه ... وما يَدْري الغَنِيُّ متى يُعيلُ
(The poor man does not know when he will become rich, nor does the rich man know when he will become poor.)
Al-Yamānī read «عَيِّلاً» with kasra on the doubled yāʾ, like سَيِّد.

semin-durr:9-9.t: His saying: {فَأَمَّا اليتيم}: accusative by «تَقْهَرْ». Shaykh Ibn Mālik — may Allah have mercy on him — took it as evidence that the placing first of the governed word does not entail [the permissibility of] placing first the governor. Do you not see that «اليتيمَ» is made accusative by the jussive verb and has been placed before the jussive-making particle, whereas if you placed «تَقْهَرْ» before «لا» it would be prohibited, because a jussive verb does not precede what makes it jussive, just as a genitive does not precede what makes it genitive? This has been discussed in Sūrat Hūd at His saying, the Exalted: {أَلاَ يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمْ لَيْسَ مَصْرُوفاً عَنْهُمْ} [Hūd: 8]. The majority read «تَقْهَرْ» with qāf, from overpowering. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Shaʿbī and Ibrāhīm al-Taymī [read it] with kāf. One says: كَهَرَ في وجهه, i.e. he frowned; and فلان ذو كُهْرُوْرة, i.e. frowning of face; and from it is the ḥadīth: «فبأبي وأمي هو ما كَهَرني» (may my father and mother be his ransom, he did not frown at me). Al-Zamakhsharī said this. The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: «It is a dialectal form with the meaning of the reading of the majority.» End of quotation. الكَهْر originally is the rising of the day with intense heat.

semin-durr:11-11.t: His saying: {بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ}: attached (mutaʿalliq) to «حَدِّثْ», and the fāʾ does not prevent that. This has already been discussed.
